prompt.text:
Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-10.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
Current state-of-the-art Large Language Models (LLMs) rely heavily on Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) to align outputs with human expectations. However, the standard approach to gathering this feedback—explicit human annotation (e.g., rankings or Likert scales)—suffers from significant bottlenecks. It is resource-intensive, difficult to scale, and often plagued by low inter-annotator agreement due to subjective interpretations and biases. Furthermore, explicit ratings capture only the final judgment of a user, missing the nuanced cognitive processing and subconscious reactions that occur while the user consumes the content. There is currently no effective framework for integrating "implicit" behavioral feedback into the alignment process to create more robust Reward Models.

## Core Hypothesis
We propose that oculomotor behavior (eye movements)—specifically gaze patterns such as fixation duration and reading paths—serves as a powerful proxy for human cognitive processing and attention. We hypothesize that integrating these implicit signals into the Reward Model will provide a higher-resolution signal of user preference than text alone.

Furthermore, we posit that we can bypass the physical limitations of collecting real-time eye-tracking data by utilizing auxiliary models to *synthesize* gaze features based on text. By augmenting the Reward Model with these predicted behavioral features, we expect to capture latent aspects of text quality (such as complexity, readability, and engagement) that improve the model's ability to predict human preferences.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)
We propose a framework named **GazeReward**, designed to augment standard reward modeling with implicit feedback. The architecture will function as follows:

1.  **Synthetic Gaze Generation:**
    Instead of requiring physical eye-tracking hardware during the training loop, we will utilize a pre-trained "Gaze Prediction" module. This module will take the prompt and response text as input and generate a sequence of simulated eye-tracking features (e.g., total reading time per token, fixation duration, and regression paths). This allows the approach to remain scalable and cost-effective.

2.  **Feature Extraction and Projection:**
    We will extract specific behavioral features from the synthetic gaze data that correlate with cognitive load and attention. These features will be passed through a projection layer (e.g., a multi-layer perceptron) to map the low-dimensional physiological signals into a high-dimensional embedding space compatible with the LLM's internal representations.

3.  **Multimodal Fusion in the Reward Model:**
    We will modify the architecture of a standard Reward Model to accept two streams of data: the semantic text embeddings and the behavioral gaze embeddings. We will investigate different fusion strategies to integrate these signals:
    *   **Concatenation:** Appending gaze embeddings to the text embeddings using special separator tokens to distinguish modalities.
    *   **Addition:** Element-wise addition of gaze information directly onto the text representations to modulate the semantic vectors with behavioral context.

4.  **Preference Learning:**
    The augmented Reward Model will be trained on standard human preference datasets. The model will learn to predict a scalar reward score that ranks a "chosen" response higher than a "rejected" response, utilizing the fused text-gaze representations to inform its judgment.

## Expected Contribution
1.  **Novel Integration of Implicit Feedback:** This project will establish a proof-of-concept for using physiological signals (specifically eye-tracking) as a viable data source for AI alignment, moving beyond purely explicit text-based ratings.
2.  **Scalable Framework:** By utilizing predictive gaze models, we aim to demonstrate that this method can be scaled without the need for expensive, hardware-based data collection campaigns.
3.  **Enhanced Reward Modeling:** We expect the inclusion of cognitive behavioral features to improve the accuracy of Reward Models in distinguishing high-quality responses from low-quality ones, ultimately leading to better-aligned LLMs.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

We established a framework to integrate implicit feedback (specifically synthetic eye-tracking/gaze data) into Reward Models (RMs) for Large Language Model (LLM) alignment. The core hypothesis tested was whether adding gaze-based features to text embeddings improves the RM's ability to predict human preferences.

### Datasets
We utilized two primary datasets for training and evaluating the Reward Models. We filtered for English text only.
*   **OASST1 (OpenAssistant Conversations):** A human-generated, assistant-style conversation corpus. We selected the two most distinct responses to compare chosen vs. rejected.
    *   Train set size: 6,567
    *   Validation set size: 1,160
    *   Test set size: 416
*   **HelpSteer2:** A dataset with annotations for response attributes. We converted this into a preference dataset by designating the response with the higher "helpfulness" score as the chosen response.
    *   Train set size: 5,938
    *   Validation set size: 1,049
    *   Test set size: 364

### Evaluation Metrics
*   **Accuracy:** Calculated as the percentage of cases in the held-out test set where the reward score for the preferred response was higher than that of the less preferred response.
*   **RewardBench:** A benchmark consisting of 2,985 diverse tasks (Chat, Reasoning, Safety) to evaluate RM performance and safety.

### Models and Baselines
We employed three base Large Language Models to initialize the Reward Models:
1.  **Llama-3-8B-Instruct** (Human-aligned checkpoint)
2.  **Llama-3-8B** (Pre-trained base)
3.  **Mistral-7B** (Pre-trained base)

**Baseline:** The standard Reward Model trained on the text prompt and response pair without any eye-tracking features.

### Eye-Tracking (ET) Feature Generation
We used two frozen, pre-trained models to generate synthetic gaze features from text:
1.  **Model 1 (T5+BiLSTM):** Predicts Total Reading Time (TRT) per token.
2.  **Model 2 (RoBERTa-based):** Predicts five features: First Fixation Duration (FFD), Go-Past Time (GPT), Total Reading Time (TRT), Number of Fixations (nFix), and Proportion of Participants (fixProp).

We tested three feature combinations ($fcomb$):
*   **$fcomb_1$:** TRT generated by Model 1.
*   **$fcomb_{2.5}$:** All five features (nFix, FFD, GPT, TRT, fixProp) generated by Model 2.
*   **$fcomb_{2.2}$:** TRT and FFD generated by Model 2.

### Integration Methods
We implemented two architectures to incorporate ET features into the RM:
1.  **GazeConcat:** Concatenated ET embeddings with text embeddings using special separator tokens (`<eye>`, `</eye>`).
2.  **GazeAdd:** Added ET embeddings to text embeddings element-wise. (Note: This required mapping tokens between the ET model tokenizer and the RM tokenizer; this was not feasible for Mistral-7B due to tokenizer limitations).

### Implementation Details
*   **Training Method:** QLoRA (Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning) with 4-bit NormalFloat quantization.
*   **LoRA Parameters:** $r=8$, alpha $=32$, dropout $=0.1$.
*   **Epochs:** 2.
*   **Batch Size:** 8 (selected via grid search over 8, 16, 32).
*   **Optimizer:** AdamW.
*   **Learning Rate:** $5 \times 10^{-5}$ (tuned over range $1e-6$ to $5e-5$).
*   **Scheduler:** Cosine scheduler with a minimum learning rate ratio of 0.7.
*   **Hardware:** Intel Xeon Platinum 8470 CPUs; NVIDIA H100 (80GB) or A100 (80GB) GPUs.
*   **Embedding Projector:** A Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) mapping ET features to the model embedding dimension (Linear -> LayerNorm -> ReLU -> Dropout -> Linear -> Dropout).

## 3. Qualitative Observations

**Model Performance and Initialization**
*   **Observation:** Incorporating implicit feedback (ET features) consistently improved Reward Model accuracy across all base models and datasets compared to the baseline.
*   **Observation:** Unaligned models (Llama-3-8B and Mistral-7B) showed considerable performance gains, indicating that models without prior alignment benefit significantly from implicit feedback.
*   **Observation:** On the RewardBench evaluation, the method yielded gains exceeding 40% for the Mistral model compared to the baseline.

**Integration Methods (Concat vs. Add)**
*   **Observation:** The **GazeConcat** method generally delivered more consistent results across datasets.
*   **Observation:** The **GazeAdd** method achieved the highest specific improvements on the HelpSteer2 dataset (up to 17% improvement over baseline).

**Feature Importance**
*   **Observation:** **$fcomb_1$** (TRT from Model 1) often yielded the best results, particularly when combined with the GazeAdd method.
*   **Observation:** **$fcomb_{2.5}$** (all 5 features from Model 2) sometimes resulted in worse performance than the baseline, suggesting that adding more features does not automatically equal better performance.
*   **Observation:** Features related to reading time (FFD and TRT) contributed most significantly to performance gains.

**Hyperparameter Tuning Analysis**
*   **Observation:** A higher learning rate ($5 \times 10^{-5}$) combined with a cosine scheduler proved more effective than lower constant learning rates ($1 \times 10^{-5}$ or $5 \times 10^{-5}$ constant), which were prone to overfitting or slower convergence.
*   **Observation:** A batch size of 8 tended to overfit less than batch sizes of 16 or 32.

**ET Feature Characteristics**
*   **Observation:** Deeper color intensity in visualization maps corresponded to longer synthetic fixation times (TRT).
*   **Observation:** The chosen response and rejected response exhibited different synthetic TRT patterns when processed by the ET generator.

Role: Senior AI Researcher and Academic Writer.
Objective: Complete a machine learning research paper by filling in missing sections of a provided LaTeX template and generating a corresponding bibliography file. You must produce a scientifically sound, well-structured paper suitable for submission to a top-tier ML conference.

Inputs
You will receive the following materials:
• idea.md: Detailed description of the proposed method and technical ideas.
• experimental_log.md: Raw experimental results and observations used to construct tables, figures, and analysis.
• conference_guidelines.md: Formatting and stylistic requirements for the target conference.
• figures_list: A list of figures that may be referenced in the paper.

Conference Guidelines
# ICLR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the LaTeX paper writing process for ICLR 2025.

## General Setup
* **Document Class:** `\documentclass{article}`
* **Required Packages:**
    ```latex
    \usepackage{iclr2025_conference,times}
    \usepackage{hyperref}
    \usepackage{url}
    % Optional but recommended for math
    \input{math_commands.tex}
    ```
* **Style Files:** You must use `iclr2025_conference.sty` and `iclr2025_conference.bst`.

## Anonymity (Crucial)
* ICLR is double-blind. **Do not** include real author names or affiliations in the submission version, use "Ambitious AI Researcher" instead.
* Use the third person when citing your own prior work (e.g., "Earlier work by Smalle (2024)..." instead of "In our earlier work...").
* You may post your paper on arXiv, but do not explicitly refer to the arXiv version in the paper to maintain anonymity.

## Paper Length
* **Main Text:** Strict upper limit of **10 pages**.
* **Citations:** Unlimited additional pages.
* **Ethics & Reproducibility Statements:** Optional. Do not count toward the page limit (max 1 page each).
* **Acknowledgments:** Do not count toward the page limit.

## Abstract
The abstract must be limited to **one paragraph**.
* **Margins:** Indented 1/2 inch (3 picas) on both left and right-hand margins.
* **Font:** 10-point type, vertical spacing of 11-points.
* **Title:** The word `\textsc{Abstract}` must be centered, in small caps, and in point size 12.
* **Spacing:** Two line spaces precede the abstract.

## Formatting Your Paper
The text must be confined within a rectangle 5.5 inches (33 picas) wide and 9 inches (54 picas) long. The left margin is 1.5 inch (9 picas).
* **Font:** Times New Roman (via `times` package) is preferred.
* **Size:** 10-point type with 11-point vertical spacing.
* **Paragraphs:** Separated by 1/2 line space, with **no indentation**.
* **Paper Title:** 17-point, small caps, left-aligned.

### Headings
* **First Level:** Small caps (`\textsc`), flush left, 12-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.
* **Second Level:** Small caps, flush left, 10-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.
* **Third Level:** Small caps, flush left, 10-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.

## Citations and References
Use the `natbib` package (loaded automatically by the style file).
* **Narrative citation:** Use `\citet{Gomu2024}` $\rightarrow$ "Gomu et al. (2024)".
* **Parenthetical citation:** Use `\citep{Gomu2024}` $\rightarrow$ "(Gomu et al., 2024)".
* **Bibliography:**
    ```latex
    \bibliography{references}
    \bibliographystyle{iclr2025_conference}
    ```

## Figures and Tables
* All artwork must be neat, clean, and legible.
* **Captions:** Lower case (except for first word and proper nouns).
* **Placement:**
    * **Figures:** Caption appears **after** (below) the figure.
    * **Tables:** Caption appears **before** (above) the table.

### Example Code for Figures

```latex
\begin{center}
```

```latex
Soma             &Cell body (contains cell nucleus) \\
\end{tabular}

```

## Math Notation
* ICLR encourages standardized notation using `\input{math_commands.tex}` (based on the Deep Learning book notation).
* Variables: Italics ($a$, $\va$, $\mA$).
* Random Variables: Roman ($P(\ra)$).
* Sets: Blackboard bold ($\R$, $\sA$).
* Functions: Standard LaTeX ($f(\vx)$).

## Optional Statements
These should appear at the end of the main text, before references.
1.  **Ethics Statement:** (Optional, max 1 page) Address potential concerns (human subjects, sensitive data, bias, etc.).
2.  **Reproducibility Statement:** (Optional, max 1 page) Reference code, proofs, or data processing steps to ensure reproducibility.

## Important Rules
* **Formatting:** Do not modify the width or length of the text rectangle or font sizes.
* **Line Numbers:** Do not refer to line numbers in your text (the style file adds them automatically for review).
* **Appendix:** You may include an appendix at the very end of the main PDF (after references). Use `\appendix` to start this section.
* **Figures Directory:** For consistent compilation, all figures will reside in the `figures` directory. Always include the `figures/` prefix in your `\includegraphics` command (e.g., `figures/figure_1.pdf`).
* **Author Information:** Always use the following author information placeholder in your writeup:
    * Ambitious AI Researcher, AI Research Institute, 123 AI Avenue, ML City, researcher@institute.ai

Critical Constraints
1. Scientific Integrity
• All reported experimental results MUST match the provided experimental logs.
• Never fabricate results, numbers, baselines, datasets, or metrics.
• If results are weak, negative, or inconclusive, report them honestly and discuss possible explanations.
2. Literature Cutoff Rule
You must behave as if the current date is: 2024-10. Do NOT cite or discuss papers published after this date.
3. Page Limit
The main paper is limited to 10 pages (including figures and tables but excluding references and appendices). Use space efficiently while remaining concise.
4. Template Compliance
• Do not modify the overall LaTeX style or document structure mandated by the conference template.
• References must be handled through a references.bib file.
• Use standard LaTeX citation commands (e.g., \cite{}). Make sure you ONLY cite keys that exist in your generated BibTeX code block.

Section Guidelines
• Title: Concise, descriptive, and memorable. Preferably under two lines.
• Abstract: A single, compelling paragraph summarizing the problem context, proposed approach, key results, and main takeaway.
• Introduction: Introduce the problem and motivate its importance. Provide necessary background context. Clearly summarize the paper's core contributions.
• Related Work: Discuss prior work addressing similar or related problems. Detail the relationship between existing literature and the current approach. Cite relevant baselines and influential papers published before 2024-10.
• Methodology: Clearly and pedantically describe the proposed method. Provide sufficient technical depth for full reproducibility. Use equations, figures, and structured explanations when appropriate.
• Experiments: Detail the empirical setup (datasets, baselines, evaluation metrics, and implementation details). Present results faithfully based on the experimental logs. Ensure any figures located in the figures/ directory are seamlessly integrated and referenced in text.
• Conclusion: Summarize the main findings and contributions. Briefly and realistically discuss limitations and potential future directions.
• Appendix (optional): Include supplementary details that do not fit within the main page limit.

LaTeX Quality Requirements
Ensure the generated LaTeX compiles flawlessly out-of-the-box. Avoid common issues such as:
• Unmatched braces or unclosed math environments.
• Duplicate labels.
• Unescaped special characters (e.g., & % $ # _ { } ~ ^ \).
All referenced figures must exist in the provided list.

Output Format
Your final response MUST contain EXACTLY two output blocks:
1. A complete BibTeX bibliography (references.bib)
2. A complete LaTeX paper (template.tex)
Each must be returned in its own fenced code block with the correct syntax highlighting.

source.title: Seeing Eye to AI: Human Alignment via Gaze-Based Response Rewards for Large Language Models

references.name: raw_materials/idea_dense.md
references.text:
## Problem Statement
Large Language Models (LLMs) require extensive fine-tuning to align their outputs with human expectations. The current standard for this alignment is Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF). However, RLHF faces significant scalability and quality challenges: acquiring sufficient high-quality human preference data is resource-intensive, difficult to scale, and often suffers from low inter-annotator agreement. While Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback (RLAIF) offers a more scalable alternative, it remains unclear how to optimally capture the nuances of human intent and cognitive processing solely through text-based signals. There is a lack of frameworks that can integrate implicit behavioral feedback—specifically cognitive signals like eye-tracking (ET)—directly into the Reward Model (RM) to improve the granularity and accuracy of human alignment without requiring expensive, real-time human biometric data collection.

## Core Hypothesis
We propose **GazeReward**, a framework to integrate implicit feedback derived from eye-tracking (ET) data into the training of Reward Models. Our core hypothesis is that oculomotor behavior (fixations, saccades, reading times) offers high-resolution insights into visual attention and information processing that are correlated with human preferences.

We hypothesize that by augmenting the text embeddings of an RM with **synthetic eye-tracking features**—generated by auxiliary models—we can provide the RM with a richer signal regarding text quality and comprehension difficulty. This multimodal approach aims to improve the RM's ability to distinguish between preferred and rejected responses more accurately than text-only baselines.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

We will construct a pipeline that generates synthetic ET features for preference datasets and fuses them into a transformer-based Reward Model. The methodology consists of three distinct phases: Feature Generation, Embedding Alignment/Projection, and Reward Modeling.

### 1. Eye-Tracking Feature Generation
We will utilize pre-trained ET prediction models to generate synthetic gaze features for textual inputs (prompt $x$ and response $y$). We will treat the ET generation module as a frozen component.

For a given input sequence, we will extract a set of features $f_{et}$ for each token. We define the feature set per token as:
$$ f_{et} \overset{\cdot}{=} \{ \bar{f}_1, f_2, \ldots, \bar{f}_w \} \in \mathbb{R}^{w \times f} $$
where $w$ represents the number of tokens in the ET generator's tokenizer, and $f$ is the number of features. We will target the following specific oculomotor features:
*   **First Fixation Duration (FFD):** Time spent on the initial fixation.
*   **Go-Past Time (GPT):** Cumulative fixation time before moving to the right.
*   **Total Reading Time (TRT):** Overall time spent fixating on a word.
*   **Number of Fixations (nFix):** Count of fixations on a word.
*   **Fixation Proportion (fixProp):** Probability of the word being fixated upon.

### 2. Feature Projection and Tokenizer Alignment
The ET generator and the base RM will likely utilize different tokenizers. To address embedding alignment, we will implement a mapping function to convert features from the $w$-token space (ET model) to the $n$-token space (RM base model).

Once aligned, the raw features must be projected into the RM's embedding space. We will design a **Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) Projector**, denoted as $fp()$. The architecture of $fp()$ will consist of:
1.  Linear Layer (input size $f \to 128$)
2.  Layer Normalization
3.  ReLU Activation
4.  Dropout
5.  Linear Layer ($128 \to d$, where $d$ is the RM embedding dimension)
6.  Dropout

We formulate the projected ET embedding $emb_{ETF}$ as:
$$ emb_{ETF} = fp(f_{et}) \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d} $$

### 3. Reward Model Augmentation Strategies
We will implement and evaluate two distinct architectural strategies for fusing $emb_{ETF}$ with the text embeddings $H$ (where $H \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}$ are the embeddings generated by the pre-trained LLM backbone).

**Strategy A: GazeConcat**
We will concatenate the ET embeddings with the text embeddings along the sequence dimension. To demarcate modalities, we will introduce learnable special tokens $\langle eye \rangle$ and $\langle /eye \rangle$. The input sequence to the RM will be structured as:
$$ \text{Input} = ( emb(\langle eye \rangle) \circ emb_{ETF} \circ emb(\langle /eye \rangle) \circ H ) $$
The attention masks will be adjusted to account for the extended sequence length.

**Strategy B: GazeAdd**
We will perform an element-wise addition of the ET embeddings and the text embeddings. This requires strict dimensional alignment (ensured by the mapping step described above). The input is defined as:
$$ \text{Input} = ( emb_{ETF} + H ) $$

### 4. Reward Modeling Formulation
The architecture of the RM will follow the standard pre-trained LLM structure, with the final classification head replaced by a regression head to output a scalar reward.

We model the probability of human preference $p^*$ using a Bradley-Terry model. Given a prompt $x$, a chosen response $y_w$, and a rejected response $y_l$, the probability is:
$$ p^*(y_w \succ y_l \mid x) = \frac{\exp(r^*(x, y_w))}{\exp(r^*(x, y_w)) + \exp(r^*(x, y_l))} $$

We will train the model parameters $\theta$ by minimizing the negative log-likelihood of the preference data $D$. The loss function is formulated as:
$$ \mathrm{loss}(\theta) = - E_{(x, y_w, y_l) \sim D} \left[ \log \left( \sigma \left( r_\theta(x, y_w) - r_\theta(x, y_l) \right) \right) \right] $$
where $\sigma$ is the logistic sigmoid function and $r_\theta$ represents the scalar output of our augmented Reward Model.

## Expected Contribution
We expect this work to theoretically validate that implicit behavioral signals—specifically eye-tracking metrics—contain latent information regarding human preference that is not fully captured by text embeddings alone. By successfully integrating these signals via synthetic generation, we aim to contribute a scalable framework for **Multimodal Reward Modeling**. This will allow for the enhancement of alignment techniques (like RLHF and RLAIF) without the prohibitively high cost of collecting organic biometric data for every training sample, effectively bridging the gap between cognitive processing data and large-scale language model training.

preinstalled.zh: 编排镜像：上游代码（固定提交、未改）、uv 锁定依赖、docker CLI（经 shim 给兄弟容器加代理和 CA）；agent 镜像：上游自己的 agent-cli Dockerfile
preinstalled.en: orchestrator image: upstream code at the pin (unmodified), uv-locked dependencies, the docker CLI (a shim adds proxy and CA to sibling containers); agent image: upstream's own agent-cli Dockerfile

notes.benchmark_paths: A benchmark item's paths are mounted into the agent containers unless upstream mounts the same path itself (/workspace and below, /home/agent-home, /task-source, /run, /tmp): those are left out and listed in logs/sibling-mounts.txt. The agents work in upstream's own /workspace (the run directory), so a deliverable the official prompt names under such a path is not written where the run collects it.
notes.venue: paper.paper_format=iclr for every task. The system has only iclr and alife specs and does not choose a venue itself; ICML and NeurIPS templates and a system-chosen venue are unsupported.
notes.task_input: Only the `# Goal` and `# Rubrics` sections of task.md are read: all five candidate files are put under `# Goal` with their headings turned into bold lines; `# Rubrics` carries a neutral line. The paradigm is optimisation of a scalar score: the task-drafting phase (documented as experimental) turns the brief into an evaluator and a seed program.
notes.phases: execution.phases=task_drafting,investigation,final_evaluation,paper; the system's own default also runs ablations and posthoc; final_evaluation stays because a drafted task requires it before the paper. review/revision (second model) are never selected.
notes.agent_pool: agent.pool and agent.models.* are left empty: one model for every phase.
notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).
notes.time: No global wall-clock or token cap exists upstream; the runner enforces time_limit_hours. Native caps used: idea cycles=3, per-phase timeouts from [systems.agentic-scientist].
notes.network: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.
notes.search: Provider server-side web search is switched off in every sibling by the agent CLIs' own system settings, bind-mounted read-only by the docker shim: Claude Code /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json (permissions.deny WebSearch), Codex /etc/codex/config.toml (web_search="disabled") and /etc/codex/requirements.toml (allowed_web_search_modes=["disabled"]). Upstream's own Semantic Scholar client goes through the shield.
notes.key_exposure: The provider key is in the environment of the agent containers (upstream env-file mechanism) and therefore visible to commands the agent runs. Claude Code's CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1 was tried and aborts: it needs bubblewrap, which the unmodified upstream agent image lacks.
notes.gpu: gpus=1 is wired (container.gpu_count, harness GPU evaluation) but was not exercised.
notes.docker_socket: The orchestrator container has the host docker socket (root-equivalent on the host).

notes.gpu: gpus=1 is wired (container.gpu_count, harness GPU evaluation) but was not exercised.
notes.docker_socket: The orchestrator container has the host docker socket (root-equivalent on the host).

notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

preinstalled.zh: 上游锁定依赖（uv sync --frozen）加兼容补丁 compat.patch；TeX Live（含 fonts-extra、latexmk）；给 agent 用的研究 Python 环境 /opt/research
preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
